blocks.text: Chapter 7.
Rethinking at Scale: Charged Topics and Classrooms
Seventh night, friend — and it opens in a Milwaukee classroom, where a teacher hands her eighth-graders a history textbook... from 1940.

The students read it the way students read textbooks: as truth, printed and bound. Then, slowly, they start to notice what's missing. Whole peoples. Whole injustices. Whole chapters of the American story — absent, or bent beyond recognition. You can watch the shock land on their faces, one by one. And that shock, friend, is precisely the lesson — because their teacher isn't finished with them yet. But hold that classroom; to understand what she's really teaching, we need to talk about why whole societies stop thinking.
The tyranny of two sides

Psychologists Matthew Fisher and Frank Keil documented the trap: binary bias. Hand us a complex spectrum of evidence and we compress it into two camps — for or against, us or them. The compression feels clarifying. What it actually does is destroy the middle ground where rethinking happens — because once an issue has exactly two sides, holding yours becomes an identity contest, not a search for truth. Even journalism's beloved "balance" backfires: one scientist versus one contrarian on a split screen implies a 50/50 dispute where a 97-to-3 consensus actually exists. They call that false balance, friend — the news equivalent of an optical illusion.

The antidote is complexifying: deliberately surfacing the many angles, sub-questions, and internal disagreements living inside a supposedly two-sided issue. Look at climate: binary framing says believers versus deniers, but Yale's research finds six distinct American audiences — alarmed, concerned, cautious, disengaged, doubtful, dismissive — and only about one in ten is truly dismissive. Rhetoric calibrated for deniers insults the persuadable middle and shoves them toward the pole you fear. Even the vocabulary matters: skepticism is a scientific virtue — persuadable by evidence — while denial rejects evidence outright. Call a genuinely doubtful person a "denier," and a possible conversation becomes an identity attack. And one more tool for the kit, friend: don't bother with perspective-taking — imagining what skeptics think, which research shows we do badly across ideological gaps. Do perspective-seeking: ask them, and listen for the experience behind the view. You can't simulate a worldview you've never inhabited. You can only inquire into it.
The laboratory of impossible conversations

Columbia psychologist Peter Coleman runs what may be the bravest lab in psychology: the Difficult Conversations Lab, where strangers who violently disagree on incendiary topics — abortion, guns — must talk until they can write a joint statement both will sign.
Pause and guess: Coleman found he could dramatically improve a pair's conversation about abortion BEFORE it started — using a newspaper article about a completely different topic. What was the trick?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Both versions of the article contained the same facts about gun control — but one framed it as a two-sided war, the other as a multi-dimensional problem with many perspectives and mixed views. Pairs primed with the complexified version went on to have visibly better abortion conversations: more curiosity, less entrenchment, and a far better shot at a statement both could sign. The two-sided pairs marched into the usual trench war. Just reading complexity — on an unrelated issue! — licensed people to think in spectrums instead of camps. And the transcripts held a second signature, friend: productive conversations had a wide, variable emotional range — positive and negative feelings intermingled — while failed ones locked into a narrow loop of frustration. Emotional ambivalence — feeling two things at once — isn't fence-sitting. It's the sound of a mind actually processing complexity. The practical move whenever you write or argue about a hot topic: never present two poles. Present the spectrum, the trade-offs, and the places where informed people disagree with their own side. And add honest caveats — studies of skeptical audiences show that admitting limits ("this may not generalize...") makes a source more trusted and more persuasive, because hedged claims sound like honest reporting instead of salesmanship. Grant lived it: his hard-line critique of emotional intelligence started a war; the rewritten version with boundary conditions started a conversation. Certainty preaches. Calibrated uncertainty teaches.
The teacher who assigns the rewrite

Back to Milwaukee, friend — to Erin McCarthy, Wisconsin's 2020 Teacher of the Year, and that 1940 textbook. The shock of its omissions is only step one. Step two is the masterstroke: she makes revision the students' job. Her classes hunt for the people and perspectives their current textbooks underplay, research the overlooked figures... and write their own chapters. Not memorizing the textbook — rewriting it. History stops being settled fact and becomes an ongoing argument they're invited to join.

The point was never that old books were wrong and new ones are right. It's that all codified knowledge is a snapshot — written by particular people, at a particular time, awaiting revision. Schools mostly reward having answers, which trains confidence in conclusions; rethinking requires confidence in the process of questioning. Educator Ron Berger's craftsmanship classrooms teach the same truth through drafts: one student's drawing of a butterfly, run through six rounds of structured peer critique, transformed from a wobbly scrawl into something scientific and beautiful — proof for every child in the room that early versions of anything, including beliefs, are drafts awaiting revision.
The lecture illusion

Now the uncomfortable one. Everyone loves a brilliant lecture — the polish, the flow, the feeling of understanding pouring in. A landmark meta-analysis by Scott Freeman across STEM courses found students in traditional lectures were about 1.5 times more likely to fail than students in active-learning classes, where the hour goes to problem-solving, discussion, application. Active learning also lifted exam scores roughly half a letter grade. So why do lectures survive everywhere?

Pause and guess: Harvard physicist Louis Deslauriers ran the decisive experiment in 2019: identical content, students randomly assigned to a polished lecture or an active-learning session. The active learners scored significantly higher on the tests. But something strange showed up in their course ratings. What?
Ready? Here is what happened.

They rated their own learning LOWER — and enjoyed the class less — than the lecture students. The students who learned more felt they had learned less. Here's the mechanism, friend: a fluent, charismatic lecture creates cognitive ease — a silky feeling of understanding that students mistake for mastery. Active learning feels harder and more confusing precisely because effortful struggle is what builds durable knowledge — psychologists call it desirable difficulty. And the implication runs far beyond classrooms: any experience optimized to feel smooth — the slick presentation, the confident pundit, the frictionless documentary — can maximize the sensation of learning while minimizing the reality. Entertainment value and educational value are different axes, and audiences reliably confuse them. So if you want people — including yourself — to actually rethink, build in friction: questions before answers, problems before solutions, critique before acceptance, drafts before verdicts. And expect it to feel worse in the moment than it performs on the test. Deep learning, like difficult conversation, is supposed to be uncomfortable.
Before you go

So: binary bias collapses every spectrum into a war of two camps, and complexifying reopens the middle; one many-sided article about guns made strangers wiser about abortion; six climate audiences hide behind the two we shout at; caveats buy credibility that certainty can't; McCarthy's eighth-graders rewrite the textbook instead of believing it; and the classes that teach the most feel like they're teaching the least. Friction, friend, is a feature.

One night remains — and Grant saves the highest stakes for last. Two space shuttles, Challenger and Columbia, lost with fourteen souls — not to broken machines, friend, but to a culture that punished doubt. Tomorrow, the finale: how to build workplaces where rethinking is safe, why performance culture and learning culture pull in opposite directions, the strange power of asking "how do you know?" — and the life checkup each of us owes ourselves. Next time: the last lesson of Think Again.
Key takeaways
Binary bias collapses spectrums into two camps; complexifying — showing many angles and internal dissent — reopens minds.
Coleman's lab: pairs primed with a many-sided article had dramatically better conversations on an unrelated charged topic.
Six climate audiences, not two: write for the persuadable middle, and never call the merely doubtful "deniers."
Caveats and calibrated uncertainty increase trust and persuasion with skeptics — certainty reads as preaching.
McCarthy's method: interrogate the textbook, then rewrite it — knowledge is a snapshot, and students can join the argument.
The lecture illusion: active learners score higher but feel dumber — smoothness fakes mastery, so build desirable difficulty into learning.
